claim: When decision makers need to select an action from a set of balanced alternatives, any tendency to choose one alternative more often (choice bias) is consistent with a bias in the sensory evidence.
source: When decision makers need to select an action from a set of balanced alternatives, any tendency to choose one alternative more often—choice bias—is consistent with a bias in the sensory evidence, but also with a preference to select that alternative independently of the sensory evidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the interpretation of choice biases, drawing from established understanding in signal detection theory and perceptual decision making.

claim: When decision makers need to select an action from a set of balanced alternatives, any tendency to choose one alternative more often (choice bias) is consistent with a preference to select that alternative independently of the sensory evidence.
source: When decision makers need to select an action from a set of balanced alternatives, any tendency to choose one alternative more often—choice bias—is consistent with a bias in the sensory evidence, but also with a preference to select that alternative independently of the sensory evidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the interpretation of choice biases, drawing from established understanding in signal detection theory and perceptual decision making.

claim: From 32 participants, 30 exhibited sensory biases.
source: We found that from 32 participants, 30 exhibited sensory biases and 15 decisional biases.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: From 32 participants, 15 exhibited decisional biases.
source: We found that from 32 participants, 30 exhibited sensory biases and 15 decisional biases.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental results from the study.

claim: The decisional biases were consistent with a criterion change in a simple signal detection theory model.
source: The decisional biases were consistent with a criterion change in a simple signal detection theory model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: Perceptual decision making, even in simple scenarios, is affected by sensory and decisional choice biases.
source: Perceptual decision making, thus, even in simple scenarios, is affected by sensory and decisional choice biases.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Perceptual decisions depend on sensory evidence.
source: This situation exemplifies a major problem in the study of perception: perceptual decisions not only depend on the sensory evidence, but also on decisional components (Green and Swets, 1966; Gold and Ding, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in signal detection theory and perceptual decision making.

claim: Perceptual decisions depend on decisional components.
source: This situation exemplifies a major problem in the study of perception: perceptual decisions not only depend on the sensory evidence, but also on decisional components (Green and Swets, 1966; Gold and Ding, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in signal detection theory and perceptual decision making.

claim: Choice biases occur in perceptual tasks even in simple scenarios in which the stimuli carry similar levels of signal relative to a neutral point.
source: Choice biases occur in perceptual tasks even in simple scenarios like the one described above, in which the stimuli carry similar levels of signal relative to a neutral point (Newsome and Paré, 1988; Mareschal and Clifford, 2012; Jazayeri and Movshon, 2007; Milner et al., 1992; Tadin et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research demonstrating choice biases in simple perceptual tasks.

claim: Choice history biases refer to how current decisions are influenced by previous decisions.
source: Choice biases are extensively studied in relation to how current decisions are influenced by previous decisions, what is known as choice history biases (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Akaishi et al., 2014; Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Braun et al., 2018; St John-Saaltink et al., 2016; Fritsche et al., 2017; Hermoso-Mendizabal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to multiple studies on choice history biases.

claim: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to repeat their previous choice.
source: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to repeat their previous choice (Akaishi et al., 2014; Braun et al., 2018), alternate between choices (Fritsche et al., 2017) or idiosyncratically repeat or alternate (Urai et al., 2017; Abrahamyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating choice repetition behavior.

claim: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to alternate between choices.
source: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to repeat their previous choice (Akaishi et al., 2014; Braun et al., 2018), alternate between choices (Fritsche et al., 2017) or idiosyncratically repeat or alternate (Urai et al., 2017; Abrahamyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating choice alternation behavior.

claim: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to idiosyncratically repeat or alternate choices.
source: Depending on the perceptual scenario, people tend to repeat their previous choice (Akaishi et al., 2014; Braun et al., 2018), alternate between choices (Fritsche et al., 2017) or idiosyncratically repeat or alternate (Urai et al., 2017; Abrahamyan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating idiosyncratic choice behavior.

claim: Whether choice history biases reflect a bias in the sensory evidence or in the decision process is under debate.
source: Whether choice history biases reflect a bias in the sensory evidence or in the decision process is under debate (Akaishi et al., 2014; Fischer and Whitney, 2014; St John-Saaltink et al., 2016; Fritsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that present different perspectives on the origin of choice history biases.

claim: Global choice biases refer to the overall idiosyncratic tendency to choose one alternative over the others, not conditioned by previous choices.
source: Unlike choice history biases, some choice biases are related to the overall idiosyncratic tendency to choose one alternative over the others, not conditioned by the previous choices. We will refer to these as global choice biases.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors to distinguish global choice biases from choice history biases.

claim: The existence of global choice biases is acknowledged in the literature.
source: The existence of these biases is acknowledged (Gold and Ding, 2013; Kingdom and Prins, 2016; Morgan et al., 2012; García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Peters et al., 2016) and they are included in current models of perceptual decision making (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Akaishi et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2018; Hermoso-Mendizabal et al., 2019), but whether they reflect sensory or decisional processes has not been, to our knowledge, assessed
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature acknowledging global choice biases.

claim: Global choice biases are included in current models of perceptual decision making.
source: The existence of these biases is acknowledged (Gold and Ding, 2013; Kingdom and Prins, 2016; Morgan et al., 2012; García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Peters et al., 2016) and they are included in current models of perceptual decision making (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Akaishi et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2018; Hermoso-Mendizabal et al., 2019), but whether they reflect sensory or decisional processes has not been, to our knowledge, assessed
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to models that include global choice biases.

claim: Whether global choice biases reflect sensory or decisional processes has not been assessed prior to this study.
source: The existence of these biases is acknowledged (Gold and Ding, 2013; Kingdom and Prins, 2016; Morgan et al., 2012; García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Peters et al., 2016) and they are included in current models of perceptual decision making (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Akaishi et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2018; Hermoso-Mendizabal et al., 2019), but whether they reflect sensory or decisional processes has not been, to our knowledge, assessed (we searched in Google Scholar several times, last one on February 2019, the following keywords: choice biases, response biases, motor biases, perceptual biases and sensory biases; we identified the relevant articles and searched within the references cited; we also tracked the articles that cited the relevant articles).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' literature search and assessment of existing research.

claim: In standard perceptual paradigms, the tendency to choose one alternative more often is consistent with a biased sensory representation.
source: The problem to identify their origin is that, in standard perceptual paradigms, the tendency to choose one alternative more often is consistent with a biased sensory representation, but also with a bias in the decision process (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Gold and Ding, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature discussing the ambiguity in interpreting choice biases.

claim: In standard perceptual paradigms, the tendency to choose one alternative more often is consistent with a bias in the decision process.
source: The problem to identify their origin is that, in standard perceptual paradigms, the tendency to choose one alternative more often is consistent with a biased sensory representation, but also with a bias in the decision process (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Gold and Ding, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature discussing the ambiguity in interpreting choice biases.

claim: Seventeen participants judged whether a grating was pointing down or up relative to a reference imagined on the right.
source: Seventeen participants judged whether the grating was pointing down or up (by pressing the down or up arrow keys on a keyboard) relative to a reference that we asked participants to imagine placed on the right at the same height of the fixation point (Figure 1A; later we will discuss Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Down and up choices correspond to clockwise and counterclockwise orientations relative to horizontal.
source: Down and up choices correspond to clockwise and counterclockwise orientations relative to horizontal.
evidence: This is a definition of the response mapping used in the experiment.

claim: Participant 12 did not show asymmetries in choice behavior (no global choice bias was present).
source: Participant 12 (Figure 1C) did not show asymmetries in choice behavior—no global choice bias was present (to see how we assessed that the bias was not significant, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Participant 2 had a tendency to give a response consistent with clockwise orientation (pressing the down key).
source: Participant 2 (Figure 1D) and 4 (Figure 1F) had a tendency to give a response consistent with clockwise orientation (pressing the down key)—that shifts the psychometric curve leftwards—
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Participant 4 had a tendency to give a response consistent with clockwise orientation (pressing the down key).
source: Participant 2 (Figure 1D) and 4 (Figure 1F) had a tendency to give a response consistent with clockwise orientation (pressing the down key)—that shifts the psychometric curve leftwards—
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Participant 9 had a tendency to give a response consistent with counterclockwise orientation (pressing the up key).
source: and participant 9 (Figure 1E) had a tendency to give a response consistent with counterclockwise orientation (pressing the up key)—that shifts the psychometric curve rightwards.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: If the bias is of sensory origin, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation should not depend on where the reference was imagined (right or left).
source: If the bias is of sensory origin, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation (asterisks in Figure 1C-F ) should not depend on where the reference was imagined (right or left).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the experimental design to distinguish sensory from decisional biases.

claim: Participant 2 exhibited choice behavior consistent with a sensory bias.
source: This is the choice behavior that participant 2 exhibited (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: If the bias is decisional, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation for the left reference should be shifted symmetrically relative to 0 deg.
source: If the bias is decisional, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation for the left reference should be shifted symmetrically relative to 0 deg (see Models).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the signal detection theory model to distinguish sensory from decisional biases.

claim: Participant 9 exhibited choice behavior consistent with a decisional bias.
source: This is the choice behavior of participant 9 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: If sensorial and decisional biases contribute, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation should be shifted, but not symmetrically.
source: If sensorial and decisional biases contribute, the probability of choosing an alternative consistent with clockwise orientation should be shifted, but not symmetrically.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the signal detection theory model when both types of biases are present.

claim: Participant 4 exhibited choice behavior consistent with both sensory and decisional biases.
source: This is the choice behavior of participant 4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Most participants showed significant biases.
source: Most participants showed significant biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across participants.

claim: About half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin.
source: About half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin and about half showed decisional biases mostly combined with sensory biases (although two participants showed biases consistent with only a decisional origin).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across participants.

claim: About half of the participants showed decisional biases mostly combined with sensory biases.
source: About half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin and about half showed decisional biases mostly combined with sensory biases (although two participants showed biases consistent with only a decisional origin).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across participants.

claim: Two participants showed biases consistent with only a decisional origin.
source: About half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin and about half showed decisional biases mostly combined with sensory biases (although two participants showed biases consistent with only a decisional origin).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across participants.

claim: Across participants, the absolute value of the magnitude of biases was larger (about 3 times larger) for the sensory biases than for the decisional biases.
source: Across participants, the absolute value of the magnitude biases was larger (about 3 times larger) for the sensory biases than for the decisional biases, indicating that the sensory biases dominated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The sensory biases dominated over decisional biases.
source: Across participants, the absolute value of the magnitude biases was larger (about 3 times larger) for the sensory biases than for the decisional biases, indicating that the sensory biases dominated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of sensory and decisional bias magnitudes.

claim: The slope of the psychometric fits provides a measure of precision.
source: The slope of the psychometric fits provides a measure of precision.
evidence: This is a standard interpretation in psychophysics and signal detection theory.

claim: Precision affects the significance level of the biases.
source: This precision affects the significance level of the biases.
evidence: This is an inference about how measurement precision influences statistical significance.

claim: The sensory biases found in the symmetric task should not remain when the same stimuli are presented but the task has two choices unrelated to the clockwise and counterclockwise alternatives, if the sensory biases were actually a complex form of decisional biases.
source: In this case, the sensory biases that we found should not remain when the same stimuli are presented, but the task has two choices unrelated to the clockwise and counterclockwise alternatives.
evidence: This is a prediction to test whether the sensory biases are truly sensory or a complex form of decisional bias.

claim: Most participants showed significant biases that include sensory and decisional biases in the asymmetric task.
source: Most participants showed significant biases that include sensory and decisional biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results for the asymmetric task.

claim: It has been suggested that asymmetric tasks are less prone to decisional biases than symmetric tasks.
source: It has been suggested that asymmetric tasks are less prone to decisional biases than symmetric tasks (Schneider and Komlos, 2008; but see Anton-Erxleben et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature, with a counter-citation also provided.

claim: Fewer groups with significant decisional biases were found for the asymmetric task (five fits) than for the symmetric task (eight fits).
source: We did find less groups with significant decisional biases (the asymmetric ones, Figure 2F) for the asymmetric task (five fits; Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) than for the symmetric task (eight fits; Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the difference was not significant (χ2 (1)=0.52, p=0.47).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data comparing the two tasks.

claim: The difference in decisional biases between asymmetric and symmetric tasks was not significant (χ2 (1)=0.52, p=0.47).
source: We did find less groups with significant decisional biases (the asymmetric ones, Figure 2F) for the asymmetric task (five fits; Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) than for the symmetric task (eight fits; Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but the difference was not significant (χ2 (1)=0.52, p=0.47).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical testing of the experimental data.

claim: Across participants, the absolute value of the magnitude of the biases was larger (about four times larger) for the sensory biases than for the decisional biases in the asymmetric task.
source: Across participants, the absolute value of the magnitude of the biases was larger (about four times larger) for the sensory biases than for the decisional biases, indicating that the sensory biases dominated (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data for the asymmetric task.

claim: Within participants, the sensory biases estimated from the asymmetric task are very similar to those estimated from the symmetric task.
source: Figure 3A shows that, within participants, the sensory biases estimated from the asymmetric task are very similar to those estimated from the symmetric task.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sensory biases estimated from the symmetric task correlated with the sensory biases estimated from the asymmetric task (r(30) = 0.81, p=2.7×10−8).
source: Across participants, the sensory biases estimated from the symmetric task correlated with the sensory biases estimated from the asymmetric task (r(30) = 0.81, p=2.7×10−8).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: What was described as sensory biases for the symmetric task had indeed a sensory origin, and not a complex form of decisional biases.
source: This shows that what we described as sensory biases for the symmetric task had indeed a sensory origin, and not a complex form of decisional biases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between sensory biases across tasks.

claim: A good agreement was found within participants between the sensory biases for the horizontal grating and the vertical grating for the two tasks.
source: We also found a good agreement, within participants, between the sensory biases for the horizontal grating and the vertical grating for the two tasks (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sensory biases estimated using the horizontal grating correlated with the sensory biases estimated using the vertical grating for the symmetric task (r(15) = 0.67, p=0.0030).
source: Across participants, the sensory biases estimated using the horizontal grating correlated with the sensory biases estimated using the vertical grating for the symmetric (r(15) = 0.67, p=0.0030) and the asymmetric task (r(15) = 0.60, p=0.015).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sensory biases estimated using the horizontal grating correlated with the sensory biases estimated using the vertical grating for the asymmetric task (r(15) = 0.60, p=0.015).
source: Across participants, the sensory biases estimated using the horizontal grating correlated with the sensory biases estimated using the vertical grating for the symmetric (r(15) = 0.67, p=0.0030) and the asymmetric task (r(15) = 0.60, p=0.015).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sensory biases are consistent with a clockwise or counterclockwise global perceptual rotation of the stimulus.
source: This suggests that the sensory biases are consistent with a clockwise or counterclockwise global perceptual rotation of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation of sensory biases across horizontal and vertical gratings.

claim: High demands on participants might have minimized decisional biases in Experiment 1.
source: These high demands on participants might have minimized decisional biases.
evidence: This is a speculation about the effect of task demands on decisional biases.

claim: Participants exhibited significant sensory and decisional biases in Experiment 2.
source: Consistent with Experiment 1, we found that participants exhibited significant sensory and decisional biases, but we did not find significant differences in decisional biases between the two blocking conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a report of experimental results from Experiment 2.

claim: No significant differences in decisional biases were found between the one reference per block and two references per block conditions in Experiment 2.
source: Consistent with Experiment 1, we found that participants exhibited significant sensory and decisional biases, but we did not find significant differences in decisional biases between the two blocking conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a report of statistical analysis from Experiment 2.

claim: The decisional biases in Experiment 2 were larger than in Experiment 1.
source: We found, however, that the decisional biases in Experiment 2 were larger than in Experiment 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which suggests that very high demands on the task like those in Experiment 1 can reduce the proliferation of decisional biases.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of experimental results between Experiment 1 and 2.

claim: Very high demands on the task like those in Experiment 1 can reduce the proliferation of decisional biases.
source: We found, however, that the decisional biases in Experiment 2 were larger than in Experiment 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which suggests that very high demands on the task like those in Experiment 1 can reduce the proliferation of decisional biases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of decisional biases between experiments with different task demands.

claim: From 30 participants with significant global choice biases, the sensory contribution was significant in all of them (94% of participants had sensory bias).
source: Taking into account Experiment 1 and 2, we have found that from the 32 participants, 30 (94%) had significant global choice biases. From these 30, the sensory contribution was significant in all of them (that is, 94% of participants had sensory bias) and the decisional contribution was significant in 15 (that is, 47% of participants had decisional biases).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across both experiments.

claim: From 30 participants with significant global choice biases, the decisional contribution was significant in 15 (47% of participants had decisional biases).
source: Taking into account Experiment 1 and 2, we have found that from the 32 participants, 30 (94%) had significant global choice biases. From these 30, the sensory contribution was significant in all of them (that is, 94% of participants had sensory bias) and the decisional contribution was significant in 15 (that is, 47% of participants had decisional biases).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results across both experiments.

claim: In standard SDT models the origin and scale of the sensory evidence is arbitrary.
source: In standard SDT models the origin and scale of the sensory evidence is arbitrary (Wickens, 2001; Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to standard textbooks on signal detection theory.

claim: The SDT model was better than the indecision model for all groups (except for participant eight for the vertical condition in Experiment 1) using the Akaike information criterion.
source: We fitted this model to the 19 groups with significant decisional biases and found that for all of them (except for participant eight for the vertical condition in Experiment 1) the SDT model was better using the Akaike information criterion (Burnham and Anderson, 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on model comparison using the Akaike information criterion.

claim: In a simple discrimination task with two symmetric alternatives, most people exhibit idiosyncratic global choice biases.
source: We showed that, in a simple discrimination task with two symmetric alternatives, most people exhibit idiosyncratic global choice biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: These biases reflect biases in the sensory evidence and in the decisional process.
source: Changing the stimulus-response mapping and testing a task with two asymmetric alternatives, we found that these biases reflect biases in the sensory evidence and in the decisional process.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study based on the experimental manipulation.

claim: About half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin.
source: Specifically, about half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin and about half of the participant biases with a contribution of sensory and decisional biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: About half of the participants showed biases with a contribution of sensory and decisional biases.
source: Specifically, about half of the participants showed biases consistent with only a sensory origin and about half of the participant biases with a contribution of sensory and decisional biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Very few participants exhibited biases consistent with only a decisional origin.
source: We also found that a very few participants exhibited biases consistent with only a decisional origin.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Across participants, the magnitude of the sensory bias was about three times as large as the magnitude of the decisional bias.
source: Across participants, the magnitude of the sensory bias was about three times as larger as the magnitude of the decisional bias.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative comparison of bias magnitudes.

claim: If a person has a bias to report that a perfectly horizontal canvas is tilted towards a given direction, it is likely that the largest contribution to the bias has a sensory origin.
source: Our findings suggest that if a person has a bias to report that a perfectly horizontal canvas is tilted towards a given direction, it is likely that the largest contribution to the bias has a sensory origin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about the dominance of sensory biases.

claim: Idiosyncratic sensory biases have not been linked to asymmetries in the neural representation of the stimulus.
source: To our knowledge, these idiosyncratic sensory biases have not been linked to asymmetries in the neural representation of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Possible asymmetries include a difference in the number of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation if the decoding is of the population-vector type.
source: Possible asymmetries include a difference in the number of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation if the decoding is of the population-vector type or a difference in the gain of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation for more general decoding schemes (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Schwartz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation about possible neural mechanisms, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Possible asymmetries include a difference in the gain of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation for more general decoding schemes.
source: Possible asymmetries include a difference in the number of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation if the decoding is of the population-vector type or a difference in the gain of neurons tuned to clockwise and counterclockwise orientation for more general decoding schemes (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; Schwartz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculation about possible neural mechanisms, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: It has been proposed that asymmetries could also emerge from the dynamics of competing neural networks.
source: More recently, it has been proposed that the asymmetries could also emerge from the dynamics of competing neural networks (Lebovich et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent literature on neural dynamics.

claim: For asymmetries to bias perception, the downstream decoding mechanisms should have not been calibrated with the environmental property to compensate the asymmetries.
source: Importantly, for these asymmetries to bias perception, the downstream decoding mechanisms should have not been calibrated with the environmental property to compensate the asymmetries (decoding ambiguity; Schwartz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about neural decoding, supported by a citation.

claim: An SDT model fitted well the choice behavior of the participants.
source: An SDT model, in which the sensory biases were included as an intercept term in a linear transduction of the stimuli (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Schneider and Bavelier, 2003; García-Pérez and Peli, 2014; Schneider and Komlos, 2008) and decisional biases correspond to a shift in the criterion, fitted well the choice behavior of the participants.
evidence: This claim is based on model fitting to the experimental data, with citations to relevant literature on SDT modeling.

claim: A model in which participants have a tendency to choose one alternative independently of the magnitude of the sensory evidence did not fit well the data.
source: A model in which participants have a tendency to choose one alternative independently of the magnitude of the sensory evidence did not fit well the data; it rather predicts an asymmetry on the lapse rate across locations of the reference that was not observed.
evidence: This claim is based on model comparison and the absence of predicted asymmetries in the data.

claim: A model in which participants guess when the sensory evidence lies within some uncertainty range was not parsimonious.
source: Finally, a model (García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; García-Pérez and Peli, 2014) in which participants guess when the sensory evidence lies within some uncertainty range was not parsimonious: first, to fit the data for the participants with pure sensory biases, the model needs that participants, when uncertain, guess the two alternatives equally often; second, for the participants with decisional biases, we found that the SDT model provided a better fit.
evidence: This claim is based on model comparison and parsimony considerations.

claim: Perceptual discrimination with two symmetric alternatives are often regarded as Type 1 tasks.
source: Perceptual discrimination with two symmetric alternatives are often regarded as Type 1 tasks, tasks for which the responses could be designated as correct or incorrect (Kingdom and Prins, 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about how these tasks are typically classified, supported by a citation.

claim: In some cases a positive signal might be perceived consistently as a negative signal (sensory bias).
source: Our results, however, suggest that in some cases a positive signal might be perceived consistently as a negative signal (sensory bias).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about sensory biases.

claim: It might be inappropriate to consider responses where positive signal is perceived as negative signal as errors.
source: Consequently, it might be inappropriate to consider these responses as errors and, in case feedback is given, provide a negative reward.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of sensory biases for task design and feedback.

claim: Perceptual discrimination tasks with two symmetric alternatives might be better regarded as Type 2 tasks.
source: Our results suggest, thus, that perceptual discrimination tasks with two symmetric alternatives might be better regarded as Type 2 tasks, tasks for which there are not correct and incorrect responses (Kingdom and Prins, 2016; Gold and Ding, 2013).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Discrimination tasks with two symmetric alternatives are commonly used to assess how perception is affected by contextual cues.
source: Discrimination tasks with two symmetric alternatives are commonly used to assess how perception is affected by contextual cues (Carrasco et al., 2004; Schwartz et al., 2007), but in some scenarios it is unclear whether the context influences perception or biases decisions (Carrasco, 2011; García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Morgan et al., 2012; Störmer et al., 2009; Schneider, 2011; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2010; Jogan and Stocker, 2012; Mather and Sharman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on contextual effects in perception.

claim: In some scenarios it is unclear whether the context influences perception or biases decisions.
source: Discrimination tasks with two symmetric alternatives are commonly used to assess how perception is affected by contextual cues (Carrasco et al., 2004; Schwartz et al., 2007), but in some scenarios it is unclear whether the context influences perception or biases decisions (Carrasco, 2011; García-Pérez and Alcalá-Quintana, 2013; Morgan et al., 2012; Störmer et al., 2009; Schneider, 2011; Anton-Erxleben et al., 2010; Jogan and Stocker, 2012; Mather and Sharman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature discussing the ambiguity in interpreting contextual effects.

claim: Even when the symmetry of the task is not broken by the context, half of the participants exhibit decisional biases.
source: Our results indicate that, even when the symmetry of the task is not broken by the context, half of the participants exhibit decisional biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings about the prevalence of decisional biases.

claim: To reliably estimate sensory biases in the presence of contextual cues, it might be better to use manipulations of the stimulus-response mapping or tasks for which the potential contribution of decisional biases is reduced or eliminated.
source: This suggests that to reliably estimate sensory biases in the presence of contextual cues, it might be better to use manipulations of the stimulus-response mapping like the one that we used or tasks for which the potential contribution of decisional biases is reduced or eliminated (Jogan and Stocker, 2012; Patten and Clifford, 2015; Morgan, 2014).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings, with citations to relevant methodological literature.

claim: The perceptual discrimination task with two symmetric alternatives is also known as the method of single stimuli.
source: The perceptual discrimination task with two symmetric alternatives that we have used is also known as the method of single stimuli (Morgan et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a statement about task nomenclature, supported by a citation.

claim: In the method of single stimuli, the decision-maker is asked to categorize the signal presented against an internal absolute reference that corresponds to a natural neutral point.
source: In this method, the decision-maker is asked to categorize the signal presented against an internal absolute reference that corresponds to a natural neutral point that the decision-maker possibly has learnt during her life (Morgan et al., 2012)—verticality or horizontality in our case.
evidence: This is a description of the method of single stimuli, supported by a citation.

claim: The sensory biases measured are deviations from the internal reference.
source: The sensory biases that we have measured are deviations from this internal reference.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the measured sensory biases represent.

claim: In the Yes-No task, decision-makers have idiosyncratic tendencies to report that the signal is present or absent.
source: For this task, decision-makers have also idiosyncratic tendencies to report that the signal is present or absent (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to classic signal detection theory literature.

claim: In the Yes-No task, it is harder to assess whether tendencies reflect differences in the strength that each decision-maker perceives or differences in how conservatively they report that the signal is present or absent.
source: Given that, in this task, there is no natural neutral point, it is harder to assess whether these tendencies reflect differences in the strength that each decision-maker perceives or differences in how conservatively they report that the signal is present or absent (Jin and Glickfeld, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretational challenges in the Yes-No task, supported by a citation.

claim: The two alternative forced choice task assesses the precision to discriminate similar orientations, but cannot measure sensory biases from verticality.
source: This task assesses the precision to discriminate similar orientations, but cannot measure sensory biases from verticality: a bias of the decision-maker to perceive orientations clockwise will affect the stimuli presented in the two intervals in the same direction without affecting the selection of the interval with the more tilted stimulus.
evidence: This is an explanation of the limitations of the two alternative forced choice task for measuring sensory biases.

claim: It is likely that participants were performing judgments of absolute orientation relative to an internal point of horizontality (or verticality).
source: Given that the reference was not physically present, we think, however, that it is likely that participants were performing judgments of absolute orientation relative to an internal point of horizontality (or verticality).
evidence: This is an interpretation of what participants were doing in the task.

claim: If participants were performing judgments of relative orientation between the stimulus and the reference, then sensory biases should not be expected.
source: As we found evidence that the sensory biases were consistent with a global perceptual rotation, if participants were performing judgments of relative orientation between the stimulus and the reference—instead of judgments of absolute orientation—then sensory biases should not be expected, as both the stimulus and the reference should be biased in the same direction.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if participants were making relative judgments.

claim: A good agreement was found between the sensory biases estimated from the symmetric and the asymmetric task.
source: We found a good agreement between the sensory biases estimated from the symmetric and the asymmetric task.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis between tasks.

claim: A good agreement was found between tasks when the biases were estimated taking into account only one localization of the reference.
source: We also found a good agreement between tasks when the biases were estimated taking into account only one localization of the reference, and thus for which it was not possible to assess the contribution of sensory and decisional biases (see legend for Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a summary of additional correlation analysis.

claim: The agreement across tasks is expected given the large contribution of sensory biases to the total magnitude of the biases.
source: This is expected given the large contribution of sensory biases to the total magnitude of the biases.
evidence: This is an inference explaining why the agreement across tasks was observed.

claim: The agreement across tasks in the spatial domain contrasts with the disagreement found between the analogous tasks in the temporal domain.
source: This agreement across tasks contrasts with the disagreement found between the analogous tasks in the temporal domain.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and findings in the temporal domain.

claim: In the temporal domain, the analogous to the symmetric task is the temporal order judgment.
source: In the temporal domain, the analogous to the symmetric task is the temporal order judgment.
evidence: This is a statement about task analogies across domains.

claim: The biases estimated from temporal order judgment and simultaneity judgment do not agree.
source: It has been shown that the biases estimated from these two tasks do not agree (Love et al., 2013; Linares and Holcombe, 2014; van Eijk et al., 2008), which suggests that decision making for time perception might be more affected by decisional biases (Linares and Holcombe, 2014; Shore et al., 2001; Schneider and Bavelier, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing disagreement between temporal tasks.

claim: Decision making for time perception might be more affected by decisional biases.
source: It has been shown that the biases estimated from these two tasks do not agree (Love et al., 2013; Linares and Holcombe, 2014; van Eijk et al., 2008), which suggests that decision making for time perception might be more affected by decisional biases (Linares and Holcombe, 2014; Shore et al., 2001; Schneider and Bavelier, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the disagreement between temporal tasks, supported by citations.
